column1: What is the standard tuning of a 4-string bass guitar, from thickest to thinnest string, and their approximate frequencies?
What interval relationship exists between adjacent strings on a standard-tuned bass, and why does this matter technically?
column2: A perfect fourth (5 semitones, 7 frets) apart. This consistency means any box shape or fingering pattern learned in one position transposes identically anywhere else on the neck.

column1: Where exactly should the fingertip land relative to the fret wire for a clean note with minimal pressure?
column2: 1–2 mm behind the fret wire. The fret wire itself stops the string against a hard edge; landing mid-gap between frets requires roughly double the pressure.

column1: What is the Franz Simandl 1-2-4 fingering system, and where should it be applied?
column2: In low position (frets 1–5), use index (1), middle (2), and pinky (4), keeping the ring finger relaxed and tucked behind the pinky rather than stretched into its own fret. This prevents tendon strain from the wide fret spacing in low position.

column1: Above which fret is One-Finger-Per-Fret (OFPF) technique considered safe and appropriate, and why?
column2: Above the 7th fret, because frets are closer together there, allowing true four-finger independence without excessive stretch or tendon strain.

column1: Why do frets get physically closer together as you move up the neck toward the body?
column2: Equal temperament divides the octave into 12 equal frequency ratios, not equal distances, so each fret marks a fixed proportion of the remaining string length — causing the 12th fret to land exactly at the halfway point (one octave up).

column1: Why is deliberate string muting especially critical on bass compared to guitar?
column2: Bass strings have roughly double the mass per unit length of guitar strings, giving them more inertia — once vibrating, they keep ringing (5–8 seconds unmuted on open low E) unless deliberately stopped. Lighter guitar strings decay faster on their own.

column1: In a walking bass line, what rhythmic role does beat 4 of a bar typically play, and why is it called 'the hinge'?
column2: Beat 4 is the approach note pointing directly at the root/fifth of the next chord on beat 1. Getting it wrong makes the chord change sound accidental, since it's the note that sets up harmonic continuity.

column1: What are the three core rules governing note choice in a walking bass line?
column2: 1) Harmonic rule: every note is a chord tone, scale tone, or approach tone. 2) Voice-leading rule: prefer stepwise motion (1–2 semitones); leaps over a fifth must be answered by stepwise motion back. 3) Metric rule: beat 1 of a new chord is almost always the root or fifth.

column1: In slap bass technique, what generates the striking motion — the thumb joint or the forearm — and why?
column2: The forearm, via pronation/supination rotation. The thumb stays rigid as a striking surface (like a drumstick tip); using the thumb joint itself is both weaker and harder on the joints.

column1: In slap technique, how does strike location along the string affect tone?
column2: Striking near the end of the fretboard (bridge area) produces cutting brightness; striking closer to the neck produces warmth and fundamental weight — this is because strike location changes which harmonics are most excited.

column1: Why does playing guitar-style One-Finger-Per-Fret technique in a bass's low frets (1–5) cause injury risk?
column2: Bass frets in that region are wider and under higher string tension than equivalent guitar frets, forcing an excessive stretch that drags the wrist out of straight alignment, straining tendons — the most common cause of beginner bassist wrist injury.
